title: Jesus wept
hookLine: at his friend Lazarus's tomb, Jesus weeps (John 11:35)
last: MORE THAN WATCHMEN FOR THE MORNING.

lines: HE WHOM THOU LOVEST IS SICK.
IT HARDLY NEEDS TO SAY COME.
cards: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." That's the whole message. Two sisters, Mary and Martha, send it to Jesus about their brother Lazarus.

They don't ask for anything in so many words. A message like that, sent from a sickbed, hardly needs to add the word come. But by the time Jesus reaches their village, Lazarus has already been in the tomb four days.

teach.b: First, the same sentence, twice. Martha hears he's coming and goes out to meet him on the road. Her first words: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died."
Later Mary comes, falls at his feet, and says the very same words. Two sisters, one sentence. Grief can find one line and say it again.
When Jesus sees Mary weeping, and the people who came with her weeping too, John says he "groaned in the spirit, and was troubled." He asks where they've laid him. They say: come and see.
Then the verse itself: "Jesus wept." No explanation, no speech. Just tears.
And the people standing there say: "Behold how he loved him!" The tears are how they see the love.

Earlier in the same chapter, Jesus told his disciples he was going to wake Lazarus out of sleep. And a few verses after he weeps, he stands at the tomb and calls, "Lazarus, come forth." And Lazarus comes out.

So in John's telling, the tears don't come instead of hope; they come right alongside it. Christians read this scene in different ways, and some find in it grief and hope standing at the same graveside.
In the story itself, the people standing by read the tears one way: as love.

how: Christians read John 11 in worship and in times of grief, and some point to Jesus's tears as a sign that mourning belongs inside faith.

games.q: you're Jesus at Bethany. Mary falls at your feet weeping: if you had been here, my brother would not have died. what happens next in the story?
o: he explains why he came late
he tells her not to cry, since Lazarus will live
he is troubled, asks where they laid him, and weeps
games.why: he groans in the spirit, asks where they laid him, and weeps, even though he is about to call Lazarus out.

practice: Let the face soften, forehead, eyes, jaw, and bring to mind a loss: a person, a place, a time of life that's gone. If tears come, let them come; if they don't, that's fine too, just give the sadness room without hurrying it along.
If you pray, you can bring the loss there without asking for anything, the way the sisters only said: the one you love is sick.
